title: “WHAT GOD HAS JOINED TOGETHER, LET NO ONE SEPARATE”—THE MARRIAGE WARNING THAT SILENCED THE TRAP AND EXPOSED THE HUMAN HEART
paragraphs: “WHAT GOD HAS JOINED TOGETHER, LET NO ONE SEPARATE”—THE MARRIAGE WARNING THAT SILENCED THE TRAP AND EXPOSED THE HUMAN HEART

They came to Jesus looking for permission to end a marriage. He answered by revealing why marriage was sacred in the first place. And behind His words was a truth that still confronts broken promises, wounded spouses, hardened hearts, and a generation struggling to understand what love really means.
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that happens when the person who once promised never to leave becomes the person you no longer recognize.
Sometimes it begins with an affair.
Sometimes with a lie.
Sometimes with years of silence at the dinner table, two people sitting only inches apart while feeling like strangers living in separate worlds.
And sometimes it begins so quietly that nobody notices.
The prayers stop.
The tenderness disappears.
The apologies become excuses.
The words “I love you” remain, but the actions that once gave them meaning slowly vanish.
Until one day, somebody looks at the person they once stood beside at an altar and wonders…
How did we get here?
Perhaps you know that question.
Perhaps you have whispered it through tears while your spouse slept beside you.
Perhaps you have watched your parents' marriage collapse and promised yourself you would never repeat their mistakes.
Perhaps you are divorced, remarried, separated, abandoned, betrayed, or still fighting for a marriage that feels as though it is slipping through your fingers.
Or perhaps you are the one who caused the damage.
You know what you did.
You know what you said.
You know which promises you broke.
And although everybody else may believe your marriage is fine, you know what happens when the doors close and the smiles disappear.
If any of this sounds familiar, stay with me.
Because nearly two thousand years ago, a group of religious men approached Jesus with a question about divorce.
They thought they were about to test a teacher.
They did not realize they were standing before the One who would expose the condition of the human heart.
And what Jesus said would become one of the most challenging declarations ever spoken about marriage.
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” — Matthew 19:6, KJV
But to understand the weight of those words, we must return to the moment when they were spoken.
The Pharisees approached Jesus with a question that sounded theological but carried a hidden agenda.
“Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?” (Matthew 19:3, KJV).
Matthew tells us they came testing Him.
This was not simply a group of men seeking compassionate guidance for troubled families.
They were attempting to draw Jesus into a controversial debate.
Among Jewish teachers of that period, interpretations of Deuteronomy 24:1 differed. Some understood the grounds for divorce narrowly, while others allowed broader reasons.
The question placed Jesus directly in the middle of that controversy.
But Jesus refused to begin where they wanted Him to begin.
They wanted to discuss the circumstances under which a marriage could be dissolved.
Jesus began by reminding them why marriage existed.
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female?” (Matthew 19:4, KJV).
Then He quoted the creation account.
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh” (Matthew 19:5, KJV; see Genesis 2:24).
And then came the declaration that has echoed through centuries of weddings, sermons, counseling rooms, and broken homes.
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6, KJV).
Read that again.
Not merely what two families arranged.
Not merely what a government recognized.
Not merely what two people celebrated in front of their friends.
What God has joined together.
In the Greek text of Matthew 19:6, the central expression is:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν, ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.
Transliterated:
Ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō.
A close translation is:
“Therefore, what God joined together, let no human being separate.”
The verb συνέζευξεν (synezeuxen) comes from a verb meaning to join together or yoke together.
It communicates a joining that is more profound than a temporary arrangement.
Jesus was describing marriage as a union established under God's design, not simply a relationship maintained as long as it remains convenient.
The command μὴ χωριζέτω (mē chōrizetō) expresses the prohibition against separating what God has joined.
And notice something important.
Jesus did not say that marriage would never encounter suffering.
He did not promise that every spouse would remain faithful.
He did not claim that sinful people would never violate their vows.
He declared the sacredness of the union and warned human beings against tearing it apart.
That distinction matters.
Because some people have used this verse to defend marriage.
Others have used it to imprison wounded people in situations where they were being harmed.
And we must never confuse those two things.
Jesus honored marriage.
He also confronted cruelty, hypocrisy, exploitation, and hardened hearts.
The same Savior who defended the sacredness of marriage never gave anyone permission to use Scripture as a weapon against the vulnerable.
But before we discuss the wounds that sin creates inside marriage, we need to understand something that many modern conversations have forgotten.
Marriage was never designed to revolve around personal satisfaction alone.
It was designed to reflect covenant faithfulness.
Go back to Genesis.
Before the first betrayal.
Before the first divorce.
Before jealousy, adultery, abandonment, resentment, and broken homes entered human history.
God created humanity and declared that it was not good for the man to be alone.
In Genesis 2:18, the Hebrew describes the woman as עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (ʿezer kenegdô).
This expression is commonly understood as a helper corresponding to him, a suitable counterpart.
The word ʿezer does not imply inferiority. It is also used elsewhere in the Old Testament to describe God as the help of His people.
The woman was not created to be an object of exploitation.
She was not created to be a servant without dignity.
She was not created to be treated as disposable.
She was created as a fitting partner.
Someone with whom the man could share life, responsibility, companionship, and the calling God had given them.
Then Genesis 2:24 declares that the two become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad).
“One flesh.”
That phrase does not erase the individuality of husband and wife.
Rather, it describes the profound unity of the marital relationship, including its bodily, relational, and covenantal dimensions.
Two distinct people enter a shared life.
And what makes this astonishing is that God established this design before sin entered the world.
Marriage did not originate as humanity's desperate attempt to manage loneliness after the Fall.
It was part of God's good creation.
That is why Jesus returned to Genesis.
He was not avoiding the Pharisees' question.
He was revealing that they had begun their argument in the wrong place.
They were asking how far human beings could go before violating the law.
Jesus was calling them back to God's intention.
And perhaps that is where many marriages begin to unravel.
Not always because people stop believing in marriage.
But because they start believing that marriage exists primarily to serve their individual desires.
When affection becomes difficult, they begin looking elsewhere.
When conflict becomes exhausting, they stop communicating.
When temptation appears, they convince themselves that their circumstances make disobedience understandable.
When resentment grows, they begin keeping records of every offense while forgetting the mercy they themselves have received.
And sometimes, without realizing it, they stop asking, “How can I honor God in this marriage?”
Instead, they ask, “How much can I get away with before I am technically wrong?”
That was the kind of thinking Jesus confronted.
The Pharisees responded by asking why Moses had permitted a certificate of divorce.
Jesus answered:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8, KJV).
There it is.
The hardness of your hearts.
In Greek, the expression is σκληροκαρδία (sklērokardia).
It refers to hardness of heart, a stubborn resistance to what is right.
Jesus identified the deeper moral problem behind the discussion.
Human beings were debating legal provisions while ignoring the sinful hardness that made such provisions necessary.
Moses' legislation addressed divorce within a fallen society. It did not mean that divorce represented God's original ideal.
And this is where the passage becomes deeply personal.
Because hardness of heart does not always announce itself through shouting.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to apologize.
Sometimes it looks like punishing your spouse with silence.
Sometimes it looks like knowing you have caused pain but being too proud to admit it.
Sometimes it looks like withholding affection to gain control.
Sometimes it looks like an emotional attachment you keep calling innocent, even though you would be ashamed if your spouse read the messages.
Sometimes it looks like pornography hidden behind a password.
Sometimes it looks like repeatedly breaking promises and expecting forgiveness without genuine repentance.
And sometimes it looks like spiritual pride.
A husband who knows every verse about submission but ignores every command to love his wife sacrificially.
A wife who speaks beautifully about faithfulness in public but has allowed contempt to poison her words in private.
A couple who can smile through an entire Sunday service but cannot speak kindly to each other on the journey home.
Not every struggling marriage involves these sins, and not every wounded spouse bears responsibility for the wrongdoing committed against them.
But wherever sin is present, Jesus calls it into the light.
And there is something terrifying about a hardened heart.
It can become so accustomed to its own excuses that conviction begins to feel like persecution.
The person confronting your sin becomes the enemy.
The truth becomes offensive.
Repentance becomes an inconvenience.
And eventually, the very person you promised to cherish becomes someone you believe you are entitled to wound.
Friend, if that describes something happening in your heart, do not rush past this moment.
Because a marriage can survive many difficult seasons.
But a person who continually refuses truth, responsibility, and repentance can inflict devastating harm.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our religious vocabulary.
He came to save sinners.
And salvation involves more than learning how to appear righteous.
It involves surrendering the heart to God.
Now consider the question that some readers may already be asking.
What about adultery?
What about abandonment?
What about abuse?
What about the person who begged for reconciliation but was repeatedly betrayed?
What about the spouse who prayed, forgave, sought counseling, and still watched the other person walk away?
These questions deserve biblical honesty, not simplistic slogans.

In Matthew 19:9, Jesus addresses sexual immorality as an exception in His teaching about divorce and remarriage. Christian traditions differ on some aspects of interpreting and applying this passage, but the exception itself must not be erased.

In 1 Corinthians 7:15, Paul also addresses abandonment by an unbelieving spouse, teaching that the believer is not bound in such circumstances and that God has called His people to peace. Christians differ on precisely how this affects the possibility of remarriage.
And although the Bible does not present a modern, comprehensive legal framework for domestic abuse, its commands against violence, oppression, cruelty, and mistreatment are unmistakable.
Psalm 11:5 speaks of God's opposition to those who love violence.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Colossians 3:19 explicitly warns husbands not to be harsh with their wives.
No one should be told that remaining physically exposed to violence is the price of honoring Matthew 19:6.
Seeking safety, involving appropriate authorities, obtaining professional help, and establishing protective separation when necessary are not acts of rebellion against the sacredness of marriage.
They may be essential responses to serious wrongdoing.
Reconciliation also cannot be manufactured by the wounded spouse alone.
Forgiveness is a Christian calling.
But forgiveness does not automatically restore trust, eliminate consequences, or require immediate access to someone who remains dangerous or unrepentant.
Genuine repentance bears fruit.
It accepts responsibility.
It stops making excuses.
It does not demand instant trust.
It does not weaponize grace to escape accountability.
And it recognizes that a wounded person may need time, safety, and wise support.
The God who hates covenant treachery does not ask its victims to pretend that treachery is love.
That truth needs to be heard.
Because some people reading this article have been carrying guilt for circumstances they did not create.
You were faithful.
You tried.
You prayed.
You sought help.
You wanted your marriage to survive.
But the other person chose betrayal, abandonment, or ongoing harm.
And somewhere along the way, you began wondering whether God was disappointed in you because your marriage did not become the testimony you had hoped for.
Hear this carefully.
A broken marriage is not proof that God has abandoned you.
Your marital status does not determine whether Christ can receive, forgive, restore, and transform your life.
And a person's suffering must never be turned into a public spectacle for people who know nothing about what happened behind closed doors.
Jesus knows.
He knows what was hidden.
He knows what was endured.
He knows what was confessed.
He knows what was never acknowledged.
And His judgment is perfectly righteous.
But there is another person reading this.
Someone who was not merely wounded.
Someone who did the wounding.
Perhaps you committed adultery.
Perhaps you abandoned your family.
Perhaps you used your anger to frighten the people who should have felt safest around you.
Perhaps you have spent years blaming your spouse for choices that were yours.
And now you are wondering whether this article has anything to offer you besides condemnation.
It does.
But the answer is not cheap reassurance.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus who confronted hardened hearts also welcomed repentant sinners.
He never taught that sin was harmless.
He never suggested that betrayal could be excused because the betrayer felt unhappy.
He never offered forgiveness as permission to continue destroying people.
But He came to call sinners to repentance.
And that means the person who has done terrible damage is not beyond the reach of God's mercy.
There is a difference between remorse because you were exposed and repentance because you have sinned against God.
Remorse asks, “How can I escape the consequences?”
Repentance asks, “How can I turn away from this sin and walk in truth?”
Remorse wants the pain to stop.
Repentance wants the evil to stop.
Remorse may cry because a marriage is collapsing.
Repentance recognizes the humanity of the person who was harmed and accepts that restoration cannot be demanded.
If you have betrayed your spouse, do not use the promise of grace to pressure that person into immediate reconciliation.
Tell the truth.
End the sinful behavior.
Accept accountability.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help.
Make restitution where possible.
And understand that even genuine repentance does not guarantee that every earthly relationship will return to what it once was.
But do not confuse consequences with hopelessness.
Christ can change a human heart.
And sometimes the first evidence of that change is the willingness to stop defending what God has already condemned.
This brings us to something astonishing about the wider biblical picture of marriage.
The story does not end in Matthew 19.
In Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul quotes the same creation passage about a man leaving his parents and being joined to his wife.
Then he says:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32, KJV).
Think about that.
The New Testament connects the one-flesh union of marriage with the profound relationship between Christ and His people.
Marriage can serve as a living witness to covenant love.
But Christ is not merely an example added to the end of a marriage sermon.
He is the center of the Gospel.
And His love reveals how different God's covenant faithfulness is from our self-centered instincts.
Jesus did not love His people because they were consistently faithful.
He came to rescue sinners.
He did not give Himself because His people had earned redemption.
He gave Himself in grace.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is the Gospel.
Not that human beings finally became good enough for God to accept them.

But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our fallen world, bore our sins at the cross, died, and rose again so that those who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
This is why Christian marriage cannot be understood merely as a legal contract or a romantic arrangement.
At its best, it becomes a place where humility, patience, forgiveness, fidelity, truth, and sacrificial love are practiced in the ordinary struggles of life.
Not perfectly.
Not without conflict.
And never as an excuse for abuse or coercion.
But as a response to the grace believers have received in Christ.
A husband who loves like Christ does not use authority as permission to dominate.
He learns to serve.
A wife who honors Christ does not have to surrender her dignity or pretend that wrongdoing is righteousness.
Both spouses remain accountable to God.
Both are called to truth.
Both need grace.
And neither can replace Jesus as the other's Savior.
That last truth matters more than we realize.
Because some marriages collapse under expectations that no human spouse could ever fulfill.
We expect another person to heal every childhood wound.
To remove every insecurity.
To understand every unspoken thought.
To satisfy every longing.
To become our source of identity, security, peace, and ultimate happiness.
But no husband can be God.
No wife can be God.
And marriage was never meant to carry the weight of worship.
Only Christ can bear that weight.
When a spouse becomes an idol, even ordinary disappointments can begin to feel unbearable.
When Christ is Lord, marriage can be received as a precious gift without becoming the foundation of a person's eternal hope.
And for those who are unmarried, widowed, or living after divorce, this truth is equally important.
You are not an incomplete Christian because you do not have a spouse.
Jesus Himself lived without marrying.
Paul spoke positively about singleness as a meaningful calling in 1 Corinthians 7.
Marriage is sacred.
But it is not salvation.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
Perhaps this is the moment to ask a question that reaches beyond the wedding ring.
What have you been allowing to separate what God calls you to honor?
For some, it is pride.
For others, secret sin.
For others, the unwillingness to forgive a repentant spouse for an offense that can be safely and wisely addressed.
For others, it is the refusal to admit that a relationship has become unsafe and requires immediate intervention.
And for many, the deepest issue is that Jesus has been pushed to the margins of daily life.
The couple still has wedding photographs.
They still celebrate anniversaries.
They still call themselves Christians.
But they have stopped inviting God's Word to correct them.
They have stopped praying honestly.
They have stopped asking whether their behavior reflects the character of Christ.
And little by little, the marriage has become a battlefield where two wounded people fight to be right instead of seeking what is righteous.
If that is your marriage, perhaps tonight does not need another argument.
Perhaps it needs an honest confession.
Not a rehearsed apology.
Not a sentence beginning with “I'm sorry, but you…”
A real confession.
“I have been proud.”
“I have not listened.”
“I have treated you carelessly.”
“I have been hiding something.”
“I have sinned against you.”
“I need help.”
Those words cannot fix everything.
They cannot erase betrayal.
They cannot replace counseling, accountability, or the long work of rebuilding trust.
But where there is safety and genuine willingness to change, they may become the beginning of a different conversation.
And if you are the one who has been wounded, you do not have to manufacture a happy ending to prove that God is working in your life.
Sometimes His work begins with courage.
Sometimes with boundaries.
Sometimes with grief.
Sometimes with repentance.
Sometimes with a restored relationship.
Sometimes with the strength to move forward when another person refuses to change.
God's grace is not limited to one particular earthly outcome.
That is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not merely a beautiful slogan.
But we must understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
He does not call evil good.
He does not erase the need for justice.
He does not promise that every broken marriage will be restored.
He rewrites lives by redeeming sinners, bringing truth into darkness, granting forgiveness through His finished work, and creating newness of life through His Spirit.
The scandal may have been adultery.
The scandal may have been deception.
The scandal may have been years of cruelty hidden behind religious appearances.
The scandal may have been the painful collapse of a marriage everyone believed was unbreakable.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is greater than the power of sin to define the eternal future of those who turn to Him.
That does not make repentance optional.
It makes repentance possible.
It does not make consequences disappear.
It means consequences do not have to be the final word about a redeemed person's identity.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
Notice where the promise is located.
In Christ.
Not in a second wedding.
Not in a new romantic relationship.
Not in public approval.
Not in the ability to convince everyone that the past no longer matters.
In Christ.
And perhaps that is the truth you have been missing.
You have been waiting for another person to change before you surrender your own heart to Jesus.
You have been waiting for an apology before you seek healing.
You have been waiting for your circumstances to become easier before you take obedience seriously.
But Christ is calling you now.
Not to deny your pain.
Not to excuse someone else's sin.
Not to carry responsibility that does not belong to you.
But to bring your whole life into His light.
The marriage.
The regret.
The loneliness.
The shame.
The anger.
The questions you have been afraid to ask in church.
The sins you have been hiding.
The wounds you have been minimizing.
Bring them to Him.
Because the cross tells us that sin is serious enough to require the death of the Son of God.
And the resurrection tells us that sin and death do not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
There is a kind of hope that depends on everything going according to our plans.
That hope is fragile.
But the hope found in Jesus Christ rests on something far stronger.
His character.
His mercy.
His victory.
His promise to receive those who come to Him in faith.
And that is why Matthew 19:6 should not merely be engraved on wedding decorations.
It should lead us to examine our hearts before God.
Are we honoring His design?
Are we treating people made in His image with dignity?
Are we practicing faithfulness when nobody is watching?
Are we confronting sin honestly?
Are we using biblical language to disguise selfishness?
Are we willing to repent?
Are we willing to seek help?
Are we willing to obey Christ even when obedience costs us something?
And most importantly…
Do we actually know the Savior whose words we are quoting?
Because you can defend the institution of marriage in public and still refuse the Lordship of Jesus in private.
You can condemn divorce while secretly committing adultery.
You can memorize Matthew 19:6 while ignoring Matthew 22:37–39, where Jesus commands love for God and neighbor.
You can wear a wedding ring while living with a heart that has stopped listening to God.
And you can carry the pain of a broken marriage while mistakenly believing that Jesus has no future for you.
The Gospel confronts every one of those lies.
To the proud, it says: repent.
To the unfaithful, it says: turn from your sin.
To the wounded, it says: your suffering is seen.
To the fearful, it says: seek truth and safety.
To the repentant, it announces the mercy of Christ.
To the lonely, it declares that you are not forgotten.
To the believer whose marriage is struggling, it calls for humility, faithfulness, wisdom, and help.
And to every person, married or unmarried, it announces that the deepest need of the human soul is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been reading this with tears in your eyes.
Maybe your spouse is sitting beside you, unaware of what is happening in your heart.
Maybe you are remembering a wedding day that now feels like another lifetime.
Maybe you are remembering the day you signed divorce papers.
Maybe you are remembering the moment you discovered the betrayal.
Or perhaps you are remembering the moment you became the betrayer.
Whatever your story, do not leave this moment with nothing but emotion.
Bring it before God.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to tell the truth, tell it.
If you need protection, seek it.
If you need wise counsel, reach for it.
If you need to begin forgiving someone, ask God for the grace to start that process without denying the truth or abandoning necessary boundaries.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not mistake religious familiarity for saving faith.
Come to Him.
Confess your sin.
Believe in the crucified and risen Savior.
Receive His mercy by faith.
And follow Him.
You do not have to invent the perfect words.
You can pray honestly:

“Lord Jesus, You know the truth about my life. You know my sins, my wounds, my failures, and the things I have tried to hide. Forgive me for the ways I have resisted Your Word. Teach me to repent where I have sinned, to seek wisdom where I am confused, and to walk in truth even when it is difficult. Heal what is wounded in me. Give me courage to do what is right. Help me honor Your design for marriage without using Your Word to excuse cruelty or condemn the innocent. Above everything else, make my life belong to You. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Be my Lord, my Savior, and my hope. Amen.”
Not because anyone needs to know the private details of your marriage.
Not because your pain should become entertainment.
But because sometimes an honest sentence can become the beginning of a prayerful community.

And if you have experienced God's grace after a season of brokenness, consider sharing a brief testimony of what Christ has taught you. Your story may encourage someone who currently believes their future is over.
You do not need to reveal confidential details or identify anyone who has harmed you.
God knows the whole story.
And perhaps someone reading the comments tonight needs to discover that they are not the only person learning to trust Jesus through heartbreak.
Not simply because it was emotional.
You may never know which struggling husband will read it.
Which wounded wife will finally seek help.
Which person contemplating an affair will reconsider.
Which divorced believer will stop believing that God has abandoned them.
Or which young person will begin to understand that marriage is far more sacred than a wedding ceremony.
We are not here merely to collect inspirational quotations.
We want people to encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, confront sin, receive biblical encouragement, and grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
These resources are meant to nourish souls, not merely fill digital shelves.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you grow spiritually, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
You do not purchase God's favor.
You do not earn forgiveness through financial support.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works or payments (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Scripture also teaches that giving should be willing, not pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you to partner with us.
Those products can become reminders of biblical truth, tools for personal reflection, or thoughtful gifts that point others toward Christ.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter the Word of God.
A person who has never understood grace.
A husband who needs to repent.
A wife who needs biblical encouragement.
A young believer who needs discipleship.
A family searching for hope.
A wounded soul who has confused the failures of human beings with the character of Jesus Christ.
Tell someone about the free discipleship resources.
Pray that the message of Christ will reach people who need truth, repentance, forgiveness, and hope.
The mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus Christ known.
And as this message comes to an end, return with me to that moment in Matthew 19.
The Pharisees approached Jesus asking when a man could put away his wife.
Jesus answered by taking them back to the beginning.
Back to creation.
Back to God's intention.
Back to the sacredness of two becoming one flesh.
And His words still stand.
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
For those entering marriage, let those words inspire reverence.
For those who are married, let them call you to faithfulness.
For those who have sinned, let them lead you toward repentance.
For those who have been harmed, remember that God's commands must never be twisted to justify abuse.
For those whose marriages have ended, do not believe that the end of a marriage means the end of God's ability to work in your life.
And for all of us, let those words point beyond human relationships to the God whose faithfulness never fails.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian life is not that every earthly promise will remain unbroken.
It is that Jesus Christ remains faithful.
When people fail, He is still holy.
When human love disappoints, His character does not change.
When sin destroys what once seemed beautiful, His power to redeem repentant sinners remains.
And when a person finally stops hiding, stops making excuses, and comes to Him in faith, the door of grace is not closed.
The cross is still sufficient.
The tomb is still empty.
The Savior is still calling.
And no matter how many chapters of your story have been stained by human failure, the final word over the life surrendered to Christ does not have to be shame.
The hands that were pierced to redeem you are still able to write a future your broken past could never have imagined.
